seoTitle: Ground-Floor Window Washing Frequency: Quarterly vs Annual Calendar
metaDescription: Ground-floor commercial window washing frequency by foot traffic, with annual spend from $360 to $3,900+. Model your schedule in our cleaning cost calculator.
excerpt: Foot traffic, street exposure, and tenant mix decide whether your storefront and lobby glass needs monthly, quarterly, or annual exterior washing. This guide turns those thresholds into a calendar and an annualized budget you can defend to ownership.
quickAnswer: Low-traffic offices (under about 200 entries per day) can wash ground-floor exterior glass quarterly or even twice a year, spending roughly $360 to $900 per year for 20 to 30 panes. Medium-traffic buildings (200 to 1,000 entries) usually need monthly service at $1,300 to $2,400 per year, while heavy-traffic, street-facing lobbies and retail-adjacent entries often run biweekly at $2,800 to $3,900 or more annually.

blocks.text: Why Frequency Is a Traffic Decision, Not a Calendar Habit

Most facility managers inherit a window schedule rather than design one. The previous property manager picked quarterly because the last vendor offered it, and nobody has revisited the decision since. The problem is that ground-floor exterior glass soils at very different rates depending on how many hands, shoulders, strollers, and delivery carts pass it every day, how close it sits to a road or parking lot, and whether it faces prevailing wind and irrigation overspray. A suburban medical office with 120 daily visitors and a recessed entry can look acceptable for 90 days. A downtown lobby on a bus route will show fingerprints on door glass within 48 hours and a road-film haze within two weeks.

The goal is to match washing frequency to the soil rate so that glass never crosses the threshold where tenants, patients, or prospective clients notice it. Washing more often than that wastes money; washing less often lets mineral deposits and road film bond to the glass, which raises the per-visit labor when the crew finally arrives.
Foot-Traffic Thresholds That Set Your Baseline

Use your access-control or door-counter data, or a simple one-day manual count, to place the building into one of three bands. Count entries through the primary public door, not total badge swipes across all entrances.

blocks.text: Notice that the per-visit charge falls as frequency rises. That is not a discount gimmick. Glass washed every two weeks carries light soil that a water-fed pole or a single squeegee pass removes, while glass washed twice a year often needs scrubbing, scraper work on mineral spots, and frame wipe-downs. Most vendors also enforce a per-visit minimum in the $90 to $135 range, so a very small storefront washed monthly may pay the minimum each time regardless of pane count.

blocks.title: Per-pane benchmark to sanity-check quotes
blocks.text: Exterior-only ground-floor washing on standard storefront panes generally prices at $4 to $8 per pane, or roughly $0.10 to $0.25 per square foot of glass, with specialty technician time billed at $55 to $95 per hour when work is quoted by the hour. A 25-pane entry at $5 per pane is $125, which lands right at a typical vendor minimum.
Building a Quarterly and Annual Calendar That Actually Works

Frequency is only half the plan. Timing within the year matters just as much, because pollen, construction dust, salt spray, and winter road brine arrive on predictable schedules in most US regions. A quarterly plan that washes in early March, right before spring pollen peaks, wastes one of your four visits.

items.name: Anchor to seasonal soil events
items.text: Schedule one wash right after spring pollen drops (late April to May in much of the country), one after summer storm season, one in late fall after leaf drop, and one after the last winter road-salt event. Low-traffic buildings on a semiannual plan should keep the spring and fall dates.

items.name: Align with leasing and inspections
items.text: If a lender inspection, tenant tour, or ownership walk-through is on the calendar, shift the nearest visit forward by one to two weeks rather than paying for an extra trip.

items.name: Coordinate with landscaping and pressure washing
items.text: Book exterior glass after sidewalk pressure washing and irrigation adjustments, never before. Pressure-wash overspray and sprinkler heads hitting glass will undo a fresh wash within days.

items.name: Set a door-glass touch-up cadence separately
items.text: Entry doors and sidelights soil five to ten times faster than fixed panes. Many buildings let the nightly janitorial crew handle interior and exterior door glass and reserve the window contractor for full elevations.

items.name: Review annually with data
items.text: Track complaints, photos, and door-count trends for 12 months. If your traffic band shifted because a new tenant or retail use moved in, re-tier the schedule at contract renewal.

blocks.text: Annualizing the Cost for Budget Approval

Ownership and asset managers want a single annual number. Convert any recurring frequency with the same month math janitorial contracts use: weekly service equals 4.333 visits per month, biweekly equals about 2.17 visits per month, and monthly equals 12 visits per year. A biweekly plan therefore produces 26 visits a year, not 24, which is a common budgeting error that leaves facility managers short by two invoices.

items: Monthly example: 30 panes at $5 per pane equals $150 per visit, times 12 visits, equals $1,800 per year.
Quarterly example: the same 30 panes with a 15 percent heavier-soil surcharge equals about $173 per visit, times 4, equals roughly $690 per year.
Biweekly example: 30 panes at $4.50 per pane equals $135 per visit, times 26, equals $3,510 per year.
Add 10 to 20 percent for after-hours or weekend scheduling if your entry cannot be cordoned during business hours.
Add a separate line for hard-water spot removal or screen cleaning, which most vendors bill as project work rather than routine washing.

blocks.text: When to Step Up or Step Down Frequency

Step up when you see recurring complaints, when a restaurant or coffee tenant opens nearby and grease aerosol begins coating glass, when road construction starts on an adjacent street, or when your building sits within a mile of the coast and salt film appears. Step down when traffic drops after a tenant departure, when you add a deep canopy or vestibule that shields the glass, or when the janitorial crew already wipes door glass nightly. A practical test: photograph the glass at 30, 60, and 90 days after a wash under the same light. The first photo that shows visible haze from 10 feet away marks your real interval.

blocks.title: Safety and insurance on even ground-level work
blocks.text: Ground-floor washing still involves ladders, extension poles, and work over public sidewalks. Require a certificate of insurance naming the owner and property manager as additional insured, confirm the vendor trains crews under OSHA's walking-working surfaces and ladder rules, and ask for Safety Data Sheets for any detergent used under the Hazard Communication standard.
Supplies Your In-House Team Needs Between Visits

If your day porter or janitorial crew handles door glass and entry touch-ups between contractor visits, stock chemicals suited to the job and the surrounding surfaces. A concentrate like Simple Green Pro HD, which is biodegradable and phosphate-free, works for degreasing concrete entry pads and dock-door thresholds where tracked-in grime ends up smearing onto low glass. Fabuloso Professional, a neutral-pH concentrate diluted at 1:64, is useful for the vestibule floor and restroom surfaces the same porter covers. For VCT lobbies inside the entry, a 25 percent solids finish such as Diversey Vectra helps the floor resist the scuffing that grit from the sidewalk causes, which in turn keeps the entry looking consistent with freshly washed glass.

faqs.q: Is quarterly ground-floor window washing enough for a typical office?
faqs.a: For a low-traffic office with fewer than about 200 daily entries, a recessed entry, and no adjacent restaurant or busy road, quarterly is usually enough, especially if the nightly janitorial crew wipes door glass. Medium- and high-traffic lobbies generally need monthly or biweekly service to stay presentable.

faqs.q: How do I convert a biweekly window schedule into an annual budget?
faqs.a: Use 26 visits per year, or about 2.17 visits per month. For weekly door-glass touch-ups, use 4.333 visits per month, the same weeks-per-month factor used in janitorial contracts. Multiply the per-visit price by the visit count and add any surcharge for after-hours access.

faqs.q: Why does the per-visit price go up when I wash less often?
faqs.a: Longer intervals let pollen, road film, and hard-water minerals bond to the glass. Crews spend more time scrubbing and scraping, so vendors add a heavier-soil surcharge of roughly 10 to 20 percent or quote higher per-pane rates for quarterly and annual service.

faqs.q: What should a window washing contract require for insurance and safety?
faqs.a: Require a current certificate of insurance with general liability and workers compensation, additional insured status for the owner and manager, OSHA ladder and walking-working surface training, and Safety Data Sheets for chemicals. Confirm whether green-certified or Green Seal detergents are required by your lease or sustainability program.

faqs.q: Should my janitorial vendor or a window specialist handle ground-floor glass?
faqs.a: Many janitorial vendors handle door glass and sidelights nightly as part of base scope, but full exterior elevations are often subcontracted or billed separately. Clarify in the scope which panes, which sides, and what frequency are included so you are not paying twice or getting gaps.
